summary:
OUTPOST is an interactive 3D Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer that lets students manage a base on the Moon or Mars. Players build essential facilities, balance power, water, oxygen and food, and protect their astronauts while responding to shortages and environmental hazards.

The game addresses the challenge by turning space-engineering trade-offs into understandable decisions with visible consequences. Building more machines increases production but also raises power demand. Storing supplies helps the crew survive disruptions. Short prompts from a robot guide help players learn through actions, while crew cards show each astronaut’s role, task and health.

OUTPOST draws on NASA resources including LCROSS, MOXIE and life-support research to explain lunar ice, oxygen production and water recycling. Its simulation simplifies these concepts for young learners while preserving meaningful differences between the Moon and Mars.

Designed for laptop and mobile browsers, OUTPOST makes space exploration approachable and encourages curiosity, resource planning and an understanding of how interconnected systems keep astronauts alive.
details:
OUTPOST — Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive 3D browser game where students become the commander of a lunar or Martian base. Their mission is to manage limited resources, build essential facilities, and keep their astronauts safe.

What it does and how it works

Players build solar arrays, ice drills, oxygen plants, greenhouses, storage facilities, and protective shelters. These systems depend on one another: machines need power, food production needs water, and astronauts need reliable supplies of oxygen, water, and food.

Players must decide whether to expand production, store reserves, repair equipment, or research improvements. Resource counters and crew health make the consequences visible. The mission continues while astronauts remain, allowing players to experiment, recover from shortages, and improve their base.

The Moon and Mars offer different conditions. For example, the lunar oxygen plant uses water, while the Martian plant produces oxygen from carbon dioxide, inspired by NASA’s MOXIE experiment. Environmental hazards create additional planning challenges.

Benefits and intended impact

OUTPOST aims to make space-engineering concepts understandable through practical decisions. Players practise planning, prioritising, and recognising how changes in one system affect the rest of a base.

The intended impact is to encourage curiosity about space exploration and STEM while helping young learners understand why astronaut survival depends on careful resource management. These are learning goals; formal educational outcomes have not yet been measured.

Tools and development

The game uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Three.js for its interface, simulation, and 3D graphics. It runs in a compatible web browser on laptops and mobile devices without requiring a separate installation. GitHub hosts the source code, and GitHub Pages provides a way to publish the playable game.

Codex/ChatGPT assisted with coding, debugging, interface improvements, and presentation content. AI-generated concept artwork was used in the presentation and labelled separately from gameplay screenshots.

NASA resources informing the game include LCROSS for lunar water ice, MOXIE for oxygen production on Mars, and Environmental Control and Life Support Systems research for water recovery and oxygen generation. Production rates, terrain, and timing are simplified for gameplay rather than presented as an engineering-grade simulation.

Creativity and design considerations

OUTPOST combines base management, individual astronaut roles and health, research, and distinct planetary environments in a compact browser experience. A robot guide provides short, action-based prompts so players learn by building and observing results.

Design priorities included scientific grounding, clear cause and effect, readable resource displays, calm colours, mobile touch controls, smooth performance, and a manageable learning curve. The goal was to preserve meaningful choices while keeping the experience approachable for junior astronauts.
